title: Building an AI for quantitative trading
author: Luccassavoia
selftext:
Hi there!
    I have a few questions and am running into some difficulties.
    I have an idea to create (or use) an AI-based program that searches for market data patterns using charts and indicators.
    My concept is essentially similar to existing software like SQX and Build Alpha.
    I want to build an AI similar to those platforms—one where I can input indicators, and it mines for trading setups and results.
    I’ve already tried using Claude and ChatGPT for research and data collection, but when I transfer the indicator to TradingView or MT5, the results don't match up.
    Does anyone know how I could set up and train such an AI on my own computer? Could you help me out with this?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the mismatch is almost always the indicator definitions, not the model. RSI alone has a few smoothing methods, so if your version uses a plain average and TradingView uses Wilder's, every signal shifts a bar or two and the results drift apart. MT5 also fills on its own tick data with spread while TradingView works off bar closes, so even identical logic gives different trades.

I wouldn't train anything yet. SQX and Build Alpha are mostly brute force: generate thousands of rule combos, backtest each one, keep the survivors, then try to kill the survivors with out-of-sample data and noise tests. that last part is really the whole product, because mine enough combos and plenty will look great by pure luck. a python loop with vectorbt or backtesting.py gets you the mining half on a laptop.

first step though: compute one indicator in python and check it against TradingView's values bar by bar on the same symbol. once those match to the decimal, everything after gets easier.

the out-of-sample part is what Quantradin does, a thing I built that paper-trades your rules on live bars so you can see whether a mined setup survives data it never saw. quantradin.com, it's free.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
Before training a model, make one “golden fixture” that runs the same rule through Python, TradingView, and MT5 on an exported slice of identical OHLC data. Compare the indicator value and signal state at every timestamp, not just final trades. Include timezone, session boundaries, warm-up length, whether decisions use the forming or closed bar, and the exact RSI smoothing method.

Once signals agree, reconcile fills separately using MT5 tick data and spread. If Claude or ChatGPT generates variants before that fixture passes, it may optimize around implementation differences rather than market patterns.

comments.author: AlphaPrimeGPU
comments.body:
Full disclosure: I'm on the team building one of these tools (AlphaPrime, GPU strategy generation and backtesting, still pre-launch), so weigh this accordingly.

The others are right that the mismatch is indicator definitions, not the AI. A few things we learned the hard way building it:

1. Parity first. Before the generator was allowed to touch an indicator, we checked it bar by bar against MultiCharts on the same data. That took longer than building the generator itself, and it's exactly the step that's failing for you right now.

2. Searching is the cheap part, validating isn't. On a GPU you can test a huge number of combos (we measured about 1.27 billion strategies in 18 hours on a single RTX 3090), and that makes the luck problem worse, not better. Most of the real work is walk-forward and noise tests that throw almost everything away.

3. An LLM is great for writing code and explaining results, but it doesn't backtest, so it can't find edges by itself.

Happy to go deeper on any of this. Not dropping a link since that's not what you asked.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Thanks for the disclosure, and the parity-first step is exactly right. On the 1.27 billion strategies figure, I'd be curious how you count that against the final survivors, since the trial count is what the significance tests need. Showing how many pass walk-forward and noise tests, and how they do on data held back from the search, would back it up. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for checking whether survivors depend on a few news days.

comments.author: SalvaFa93
comments.body:
Il punto che descrivi alla fine, l'indicatore che su TradingView o MT5 dà numeri diversi dal tuo codice, quasi mai dipende dall'IA. Le due piattaforme non ti danno le stesse barre: prezzo denaro contro lettera, orario del server del broker, festività, volumi tick. E le formule non sono le stesse: RSI e ATR di TradingView usano la media di Wilder, non la EMA (è nella documentazione di Pine Script, funzioni ta.rsi e ta.atr), e i primi valori di qualsiasi media dipendono da quante barre di storico hai caricato. Finché non confronti i tuoi numeri con le barre esportate dalla stessa piattaforma su cui poi vuoi usare l'indicatore, non saprai mai se il problema è il codice o il confronto.



Sul resto, un consiglio da chi ci lavora: costruire qualcosa come SQX o Build Alpha non è un progetto da weekend, e la parte difficile non è trovare schemi nei dati ma capire quali sono rumore. Prima di addestrare qualsiasi cosa, fai tornare un indicatore semplice fra il tuo codice e la piattaforma: se non torna quello, non tornerà niente di quello che ci costruisci sopra.

replies.author: SalvaFa93
replies.body: Vero, e non è nemmeno colpa loro: i corsi vendono il modello e saltano la parte sui dati, che è noiosa e non si mette in una slide. Il lato buono è che il confronto barra per barra lo fa chiunque in un pomeriggio, senza sapere niente di IA, e dice subito se ha senso andare avanti. Chi lo salta scopre il problema dopo, quando ha già un modello addestrato su numeri sbagliati.

replies.author: SalvaFa93
replies.body: Nessuno in particolare, e non farei nomi: è una struttura, non un corso. Quasi tutto quello che si vende sui social come "IA per il trading" parte già dal modello, perché è la parte che si mostra bene, e tratta i dati come un dettaglio da scaricare. Se vuoi una fonte seria sul tema, il libro di López de Prado (Advances in Financial Machine Learning) dedica i primi capitoli proprio a come si preparano i dati prima di toccare un modello: è l'opposto dell'ordine che vedi nei corsi, ed è il motivo per cui i risultati poi non tornano.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good point on Wilder smoothing and the bars differing between platforms. I'd add that the comparison should use bars exported from the same platform, checking one simple indicator first and then everything else. Once the mining starts, keep a period of data that's never touched and count how many combinations were tried. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases and earnings) is one source you could use to check whether the results depend on a few news days.

replies.author: SalvaFa93
replies.body: D'accordo su tutto, e il punto che quasi nessuno tiene è l'ultimo: contare quante combinazioni hai provato. Senza quel numero, il periodo lasciato da parte serve a poco, perché prima o poi una combinazione lo passa per caso. Sullo strumento che citi non mi esprimo: non l'ho usato.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Exactly, and that trial count is also what lets you judge whether a surviving combination is real, since the more you test, the more likely one passes by chance. Fair enough on the tool, no need to have used it. Thanks for the discussion.

comments.author: drhobbi
comments.body:
I'm building https://canglerlabs.au/ and happy to share tips and lessons learned 

Here are my top 5  
1. Focus on data quality and build a bi-temporal data store for point in time integrity  
2. Handle survivorship and look ahead bias via a framework  
3. Build a harness for building your platform  
4. Use CI CD with deterministic tests to handle hallucinations   
5. Build a comprehensive simulation framework that checks for false alpha. Your goal is not to find alpha but prove alpha is not real so when you do find it you can have confidence your model won't crash when you deploy it live
